title: Reconstruct Original Digits from English
statement:
Someone took a collection of digits (each from 0 to 9, repeats allowed), spelled each one as its lowercase English word (`"zero"`, `"one"`, `"two"`, `"three"`, `"four"`, `"five"`, `"six"`, `"seven"`, `"eight"`, `"nine"`), joined the words, and then scrambled all the letters. The result is `s`.

Return the original digits as a string, sorted from smallest to largest. `s` is guaranteed to have been produced this way.
constraints: Each character of s is one of e, f, g, h, i, n, o, r, s, t, u, v, w, x, z
s is a scrambled concatenation of digit words
notes:
## Intuition

Five digit words contain a letter that no other digit word uses: `z` only in "zero", `w` only in "two", `u` only in "four", `x` only in "six" and `g` only in "eight". Counting those letters gives those five digits immediately. Once they are known, more letters become unique among what is left: `h` appears only in "three" and "eight", `f` only in "four" and "five", `s` only in "six" and "seven", `o` in "zero", "one", "two" and "four", and `i` in "five", "six", "eight" and "nine". Subtracting the known digits gives the rest. (A slower way peels whole words off the letter counts in the same safe order.)

## Approach

1. Count every letter of `s` in `freq`.
2. Set `digits[0]`, `digits[2]`, `digits[4]`, `digits[6]`, `digits[8]` from the counts of `z`, `w`, `u`, `x`, `g`.
3. `digits[3] = count(h) - digits[8]`, `digits[5] = count(f) - digits[4]`, `digits[7] = count(s) - digits[6]`.
4. `digits[1] = count(o) - digits[0] - digits[2] - digits[4]` and `digits[9] = count(i) - digits[5] - digits[6] - digits[8]`.
5. Build `result` by writing each digit from 0 to 9 as many times as it occurs.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "owoztneoer"` has `z = 1`, `w = 1`, `o = 3`, `h = 0` and no `u`, `x`, `g`, `f`, `s` or `i`. So `digits[0] = 1` and `digits[2] = 1`, every other first-pass digit is 0, and `digits[1] = 3 - 1 - 1 - 0 = 1`. The rest stay 0, giving `"012"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) to count the letters; the rest is constant work plus writing the answer, which is shorter than `s`.
- Space: O(1) for the counts (at most 15 distinct letters), plus the output string.

## Pitfalls

- The order matters: `digits[1]`, `digits[3]`, `digits[5]`, `digits[7]` and `digits[9]` depend on digits that must already be known.
- Greedily removing words in 0-to-9 order fails: on `"twonine"`'s letters, taking "one" first uses up the `o` that "two" needs.
- Pick letters that separate the words cleanly. `n`, for example, appears twice in "nine" and once in "one" and "seven", so it is easy to subtract wrongly; `i` is safer for nine.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `freq` | how many times each letter appears in `s` |
| `count(letter)` | `freq[letter]`, or 0 if the letter is absent |
| `digits` | `digits[d]` is how many times digit `d` was spelled out |
| `result` | the sorted digits being written out |

narration.3: Go through every letter of the scrambled string.
narration.4: Count how many times this letter appears.
narration.6: count returns a letter's total, or 0 when it never appears.
narration.8: Only "zero" has a z, so each z is one zero.
narration.13: h is in three and eight; remove the eights to leave the threes.
narration.14: f is in four and five; remove the fours to leave the fives.
narration.15: s is in six and seven; remove the sixes to leave the sevens.
narration.16: o is in zero, one, two and four; what remains after those three belongs to one.
narration.17: i is in five, six, eight and nine; what remains belongs to nine.
narration.19: Write the digits from smallest to largest.
narration.20: Append this digit as many times as it was spelled out.
